summary: Reports on the status of 11 different implementations of the Ethernet MIB by 7 vendors on 7 Ethernet interface chips. It is informational and shares lessons learned.

eli5.summary: A report from companies that built the same Ethernet readings, comparing notes about what worked and what was tricky.

questions: which ethernet mib variables were deprecated
subtitle: A 1992 report on which Ethernet MIB variables vendors actually built, and what the working group decided to drop.

tldr.problem: The Ethernet MIB working group needed evidence on which MIB variables were really implemented, since some mandatory variables were optional in the IEEE 802.3 specification.
tldr.mechanism: The author tabulates vendor-supplied data on 11 implementations by 7 vendors on 7 Ethernet chips, draws conclusions, and records the working group's recommendations.
tldr.outcome: The group recommended deprecating several rarely implemented objects and keeping the collision histogram table as an optional group. The memo is informational and not a standard.

today: RFC 1369 is an Informational memo, not a standard, and the unit metadata shows no RFC obsoleting or updating it. It is a snapshot of Ethernet MIB implementation experience from October 1992.

sections.title: Purpose of the Report
sections.content:
The Ethernet MIB Working Group was given two tasks: explain why some variables that are optional in the IEEE 802.3 specification got MANDATORY status in the Internet Ethernet MIB, and produce an implementation report. Neither document is on the standards track.

The report covers variables implemented in Ethernet interface chips and in software drivers, and summarizes field experience, especially for variables in dispute. It reflects 11 implementations of the MIB by 7 vendors on 7 Ethernet interface chips, and was meant to be updated while the MIB moved through standardization.
sections.eli5: Some companies built the same set of Ethernet counters. This paper checks which ones they really built so the list can be made sensible.

sections.title: Observations from the Data
sections.content:
Only 4 variables are implemented in every implementation: AlignmentErrors, FCSErrors, ExcessiveCollisions and InternalMacTransmitErrors. Five more are in all but one: SingleCollisionFrames, MultipleCollisionFrames, LateCollisions, FrameTooLongs and CarrierSenseErrors.

Where a variable is missing from one implementation, the author often finds the same chip supports it elsewhere. For example, implementation 3 lacks SingleCollisionFrames although other AMD LANCE implementations (7, 8 and 10) have it, so the chip can provide it. FrameTooLongs is easily kept by software as a driver-level function.

Of the 22 variables, 11 were implemented in about half or fewer of the implementations. Each implementation provides between 11 and 16 variables, an average of 12.8. The two IEEE 802.3 encapsulation-specific variables appear in 2 and 0 implementations.
sections.eli5: Only a few counters were built by everybody. When one company skipped a counter that others built on the same chip, it was usually just a choice, not a limit of the hardware.

sections.title: Conclusions
sections.content:
The control variables such as InitializeMac are not widely implemented, possibly because vendors avoid writable variables until security is in place. One vendor found them hard to implement and not useful, and recommended dropping them.

The two 802.3 encapsulation variables and the collision histogram variables are barely implemented. The author supports moving the first pair to an optional group, and the histogram variables already sit in their own optional group.

Of the remaining 13 statistical variables, 9 are in 10 or 11 implementations. SQETestErrors and ExcessiveDeferrals are in 3 and 1. DeferredTransmissions and InternalMacReceiveErrors are in 8 or 9, which the author attributes to local implementation choices rather than a lack of support. The suggested options are to split the statistics group so the two rare variables are optional, or to remove them.
sections.eli5: Counters that nearly everyone built are clearly useful. Counters almost nobody built might belong in an optional bin, or be thrown out.

sections.title: Final Action
sections.content:
At the San Diego IETF Meeting on 17 March 1992 the working group made six recommendations:

  • dot3TestTdrValue is deprecated; it has effectively no implementations and some chips return a wrong value.
  • dot3StatsInRangeLengthErrors and dot3StatsOutOfRangeLengthFields are deprecated.
  • dot3InitializeMac, dot3MacSubLayerStatus, dot3MulticastReceiveStatus and dot3TxEnabled are deprecated.
  • dot3StatsExcessiveDeferrals is deprecated; only one system implemented it and its definition was questioned.
  • dot3StatsSQETestErrors is kept, because some transceiver and cable errors can only be detected with this counter.
  • The collision histogram table dot3CollTable stays as an optional group.
sections.eli5: The group threw out the counters nobody used, but kept one rarely built counter because it catches problems nothing else can.

sections.title: The Implementation Table
sections.content:
The raw data is a table with one column per implementation and one row per MIB variable. Each cell is a code: Y for fully implemented, N for not implemented (it would return a noSuchName error), and C for implemented but returning a constant, with a badValue error for any set to a different value.

Footnotes explain quirks, such as an implementation that does not run a TDR test but reports the TDR value from the last collision, or one that detects a variable solely in software. The chips listed include the Intel 82586, Fujitsu 86950, Sonic, AMD Lance, National NIC 8390C, Intel 82596 and AMD ILACC. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: A big grid shows each company down one side and each counter across the top, with a letter saying whether the counter really worked, was missing, or was faked with a fixed number.

viz.caption: CODES USED IN THE IMPLEMENTATION TABLE (RFC 1369)

items.label: Fully implemented
items.desc: Reports a truthful count or state; writable variables accept all values.

items.label: Not implemented
items.desc: Would return a noSuchName error if accessed.

items.label: Constant
items.desc: Returns a constant for gets and a badValue error for sets to any other value.
